title: How to Grill Perfect Pork Tenderloin: Temp and Timing Guide
meta_description: Learn how to grill juicy pork tenderloin every time. Our guide covers the perfect grilled pork tenderloin internal temp, timing, and preparation tips.
html:
Pork tenderloin is one of the most forgiving and versatile cuts of meat you can throw on the grill, but it has a reputation for drying out faster than a summer sidewalk. The problem usually isn't the seasoning or the heat source—it is the lack of precision. If you want juicy, pink-in-the-middle results, you need to stop guessing by time or feel and start using a thermometer. Getting the right grilled pork tenderloin internal temp is the single most effective way to ensure dinner is a success.

Why Temperature Matters More Than Time

Recipes often give specific cooking times, such as "grill for 15 minutes." However, every grill runs differently, and tenderloins vary in thickness. A thin piece might cook in ten minutes, while a thicker one could take twenty. Relying solely on a clock is a recipe for overcooked meat.

Connective tissue breaks down and muscle fibers contract as meat heats up. Push pork past its ideal temperature, and those fibers squeeze out every drop of moisture. This is why we recommend grabbing an Instant-Read Meat Thermometer. Nail the perfect temp every time — fast digital thermometers for grilling, roasting, and frying eliminate the guesswork completely.

The Target: Grilled Pork Tenderloin Internal Temp

So, what is the magic number? The USDA currently recommends a safe internal temperature of 145°F for whole cuts of pork, followed by a three-minute rest period. This is a change from the old "well-done" standard of 160°F, which resulted in the dry, gray pork many of us grew up eating.

For the best eating experience, you should actually pull your pork off the grill when it hits 140°F. Why? Because of "carryover cooking." The residual heat inside the meat continues to cook the tenderloin after you remove it from the fire. The temperature will rise about 5 to 10 degrees while it rests, landing it perfectly at 145°F. If you wait until it hits 145°F on the grill, you will end up with meat closer to 155°F, which is starting to dry out.

Prep and Seasoning for Success

Before you even think about heat, you need to prep the meat. Tenderloins often come with a silverskin—a tough, silvery layer of connective tissue on one side. If you leave this on, it will shrink and cause the meat to curl up on the grill, leading to uneven cooking. Use a sharp knife to slide under the silverskin and slice it off.

For seasoning, keep it simple but bold. Because pork is mild, it pairs well with savory and sweet flavors. A simple rub of brown sugar, smoked paprika, garlic powder, salt, and pepper works wonders. Apply the rub generously just before grilling. If you are using a wet marinade, try to pat the meat dry before it hits the grates to ensure you get a good sear.

The Two-Zone Grilling Method

Tenderloins are lean and relatively small, so they can burn quickly on the outside before the inside is done. To prevent this, set up your grill for two-zone cooking. This means piling the coals (or turning on the burners) on one side to create a hot zone, and leaving the other side empty for a cool zone.

Sear the meat over the hot side first to get those flavorful grill marks and a caramelized crust. Once seared on all sides, move the tenderloin to the cool side. Close the lid and let it roast gently with indirect heat until it reaches that target grilled pork tenderloin internal temp.

  1. Sear: Place tenderloin over direct heat. Turn every 2 minutes until browned on all sides (approx. 6-8 minutes total).
  2. Move: Transfer meat to the indirect heat side of the grill.
  3. Cook: Close the lid. Cook for another 10-15 minutes, checking the temp frequently.
  4. Check: Insert your Instant-Read Meat Thermometer into the thickest part of the meat.
  5. Rest: Remove at 140°F and tent loosely with foil.

Resting: The Final Step

You might be tempted to slice into the meat immediately, but patience is key. Resting allows the juices, which have been driven to the center of the meat by the heat, to redistribute back throughout the tenderloin. If you cut too soon, those juices will pool on your cutting board rather than staying in your mouth.

Tent the meat loosely with foil and let it sit for at least 5 to 10 minutes. During this time, the temperature will climb to the safe USDA standard of 145°F. When you finally slice it, you should see a faint blush of pink in the center, indicating tender, juicy meat.

FAQ

Is it safe to eat pork tenderloin that is pink in the middle?

Yes, absolutely. As long as the meat has reached an internal temperature of 145°F and rested for 3 minutes, a slight pink color is safe and indicates the meat is juicy and not overcooked.

How long does it take to grill a pork tenderloin?

It generally takes about 15 to 20 minutes total. However, relying on time rather than the grilled pork tenderloin internal temp is risky. Always use a thermometer to be sure.

Should I use a gas or charcoal grill?

You can use either. Gas offers easier temperature control, while charcoal provides a smokier flavor. Regardless of the fuel source, use a two-zone setup and an instant-read thermometer for the best results.
